questions.q: What does the type argument in db.query<Order>("select * from orders") guarantee?
questions.explain: The driver cannot know what a SQL string returns when TypeScript compiles. The type argument only tells the compiler what to assume; the lesson's first example compiled and then crashed.
options: That the rows are validated against Order at runtime
That the SQL is checked against the database schema at compile time
Nothing about the data: it is an unchecked promise, like an as assertion
That columns are renamed to match Order's properties

questions.q: With the pg driver, what JavaScript value does a bigint column (or count(*)) arrive as?
questions.explain: 64-bit integers can exceed JavaScript's safe integer range, so pg returns them as text by default. PGlite returns a number when it is safe and a bigint otherwise. The row type must match the driver you use.
options: A number when small and a string when large

questions.q: Why do both drivers return numeric columns as strings?
questions.explain: numeric exists for exact decimals, such as money. Converting to a float would undo that. Keep the string and parse it exactly, or use a decimal library.
options: Because PostgreSQL stores them as text
Because a JavaScript number is binary floating point and could silently lose exact decimal digits
Because strings are faster to transfer
It is a bug that will be fixed

questions.q: A server in Lagos reads a date column holding 2026-09-24 with the pg driver and calls toISOString(). It prints 2026-09-23T23:00:00.000Z. Why?
questions.explain: A calendar date has no time zone, but a JavaScript Date is a moment. Keep date columns as "YYYY-MM-DD" strings (a custom type parser) or run servers in UTC, and be deliberate about the conversion.
options: The database stored the wrong date
pg turns a date into a Date at local midnight, which in Lagos (UTC+1) is 23:00 UTC the day before
PostgreSQL dates are always one day behind

questions.q: A column note text allows nulls. How should the row type declare it?
questions.explain: Every column is present in every row; a missing value is null. ? means "the property may be absent" and says nothing about null, so it would let row.note.trim() compile on a null.

questions.q: What is the difference between a row type and an entity in the lesson?
questions.explain: Keeping them apart puts every awkward conversion (snake_case, bigint strings, money) in one mapper per table, and keeps the rest of the application free of driver details.
options: They are two names for the same thing
The row type mirrors the database exactly (names, nulls, driver value types); the entity is the application's own model, produced by a mapper that renames and converts
The entity is generated; the row type is written by hand
The row type is for inserts, the entity for selects

questions.q: Why does the lesson's toKobo throw instead of returning Number(value) for any input?
questions.explain: For money, a wrong number is worse than an error. The mapper is the boundary where database values become trusted application values, so that is where to refuse bad ones.
options: An unsafe integer would be silently rounded; failing at the mapper points straight at the bad data instead of producing a wrong amount somewhere else

questions.q: Which type should a GET /customers/:id handler return?
questions.explain: A response DTO is the contract with the client. Building a new object is what actually removes secret fields; a type like Omit only hides them from the compiler.
options: The CustomerRow, so the client sees the real data
A CustomerResponse DTO built field by field from the entity, without passwordHash

questions.q: function toResponse(c: Customer): CustomerResponse { return c; } compiles although Customer has a passwordHash. Why?
questions.explain: Assignability asks "does it have at least these properties?". The returned object is still the full entity at runtime, so the hash leaks into the JSON.
options: TypeScript is structural: a value with all the required properties fits the type, extra properties included
Because the function has no body

questions.q: When does TypeScript's excess property check catch an extra property such as passwordHash?
questions.explain: The check applies to object literals only, and properties that come in through a spread are not checked as excess. That is why mappers list fields one by one.
options: Always, whenever a value is assigned to a type
When the property is written directly in a fresh object literal assigned to the target type
When the property comes from a spread { ...customer }

questions.q: What does Partial<Pick<CreateCustomerInput, "fullName" | "phone">> express for an update endpoint?
questions.explain: Pick selects what may change at all; Partial makes each optional. email and password are not part of the type, so this path cannot change them.
options: Only fullName and phone can be changed, and each is optional in a PATCH
The password can be updated optionally

questions.q: When is it worth validating rows from your own database at runtime?
questions.explain: Constraints guarantee some things, not your TypeScript types: a new status value, a column made nullable, or an old jsonb shape all pass the database's checks. Validate at the boundary where drift would hurt.
options: Where types can drift from reality and mistakes are costly: tables other systems write, jsonb columns, rows that feed money decisions

questions.q: Why does the validation example query with db.query<unknown>(…)?
questions.explain: With unknown, TypeScript refuses row.status until a check narrows the type. The schema's safeParse then returns typed data or a list of issues.
options: It is the honest type before validation, and it forces the code through the schema before any field can be used

questions.q: What does type OrderRow = z.infer<typeof OrderRowSchema> give you?
questions.explain: Writing the shape once, as a schema, and deriving the type from it removes the risk of a type saying one thing while the validator checks another.
options: A runtime copy of the schema
A TypeScript type derived from the schema, so the runtime check and the static type cannot disagree

questions.q: Why does findById return Promise<Order | undefined> instead of Promise<Order>?
questions.explain: With strictNullChecks, (await findById(id)).status does not compile; the caller must check and answer 404 or similar. Failures (a lost connection) are still exceptions.
options: Because TypeScript cannot type promises precisely
"Not found" is a normal outcome, and the union forces every caller to handle it before using the order
So it can be used with await

questions.q: What does a branded OrderId type cost at runtime?
questions.explain: Brand<number, "OrderId"> intersects number with a phantom property the compiler tracks. At runtime orderId(5) is just 5, but a CustomerId can no longer be passed where an OrderId is expected.
options: A validation call on every use
Nothing: the brand exists only in types; the value is a plain number
A symbol property on each id

questions.q: Why does the repository map an OrderSort union to fixed SQL strings instead of accepting a column name?
questions.explain: The union makes invalid sorts a compile error, and the Record<OrderSort, string> makes a new sort option without SQL a compile error too. At runtime, input from a query string must still be checked against the same list.
options: Because order by is slow with parameters
Identifiers cannot be $1 parameters, so they are pasted into SQL; mapping a closed set of names to fixed fragments means user input can never become SQL

questions.q: The repository's constructor takes a Queryable instead of a PGlite. What does that enable?
questions.explain: Depending on the smallest interface you need (dependency inversion) lets the caller decide the connection. Inside db.transaction(async (tx) => …), repositories built on tx all commit or roll back together.
options: The same repository can run on the database, inside a transaction (tx), or on a pg pool, so several repositories can share one transaction

questions.q: How does the lesson propose to stop generated row types from drifting from the schema?
questions.explain: A drift check turns "someone forgot to update the types" into a failing build, next to the migration that caused it.
options: Regenerate them by hand every month
Commit the generated file and, in CI, regenerate it from a freshly migrated database and fail the build if it differs
Generate them in production at startup

questions.q: The generator typed orders.status as string, not "pending" | "paid" | …. Why?
questions.explain: A PostgreSQL enum type or a lookup table with a foreign key carries the allowed values in the schema itself, where tools can see them. With a check constraint, you narrow the type by hand.
options: information_schema.columns only knows the column is text; the allowed values live in a check constraint the generator does not read

questions.q: In the tiny query builder, what is the result type of selectFrom(db, "orders", ["id", "total_kobo"])?
questions.explain: The column list is inferred as the literal union "id" | "total_kobo", constrained to the table's keys, and Pick builds the result type from exactly those columns.

questions.q: Which risk is typical of ORMs and must still be watched for?
questions.explain: ORMs save a lot of code, but the database work still happens. Log or inspect the generated SQL, check pg_stat_statements, and drop to raw SQL where you need precise control.
options: Hidden SQL: loading related records in a loop can run one query per row (N+1), and locking or plan details are less visible

questions.q: How should the login code get a customer's password_hash?
questions.explain: Data that is never loaded cannot leak. Keeping secrets out of the widely used entity reduces the places where a mistake could expose them.
options: Load it with every customer so it is always available
Select it only in the login query, into its own small type, so ordinary customer entities never carry it
Store it in the response DTO but hide it in the UI

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type argument renames nothing. The row has the database's price_kobo, so priceKobo is undefined, and TypeScript accepted it because it trusted <Product>.

questions.q: What does this print with PGlite?
questions.explain: PGlite returns a bigint column as a number when the value is a safe integer and as a JavaScript bigint when it is not. So the honest row type is number | bigint. (pg would print string three times.)

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: numeric arrives as strings, so + concatenates them. The row type says string, which is exactly what makes this bug visible to anyone reading the code; typing it as number would hide it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON has null but no undefined: properties set to undefined are dropped. A nullable column should stay null so clients can tell "no phone" from "phone not included".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The spread copies every property of the entity, and TypeScript does not treat spread properties as excess, so it compiles and the hash goes out. List fields explicitly instead.
options: A compile error: passwordHash does not exist in CustomerSummary

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Brands vanish when TypeScript is compiled: the ids are plain numbers, serialise as numbers, and compare equal. The protection is entirely at compile time, and it costs nothing at runtime.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A string or bigint that holds a safe whole number converts exactly. Half a kobo and a number beyond 253 are refused rather than rounded.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: nullable() allows null but not a missing property, so row 2 fails on phone, just as a real row always has every column. Row 3 has the id as a string, as a pg bigint would, and fails on id.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: udt_name uses PostgreSQL's internal type names (int4, int8), which is what a generator maps. A primary key is implicitly not null; columns without not null report YES and become | null in the generated type.

questions.q: Write toCamelKeys(row) that returns a new object with every snake_case key turned into camelCase, keeping the values (including null) unchanged.
questions.explain: A generic renamer is handy, but notice its return type: Record<string, unknown>. It cannot know the entity's type, which is why the lesson writes one typed mapper per table and converts values there too.
questions.expected:
{
  id: 1,
  customerId: 7,
  totalKobo: 450000,
  note: null,
  placedAtUtc: '2026-09-20'
}

questions.q: numeric(12, 2) amounts arrive as strings such as "1150.15". Write nairaToKobo(amount) that converts exactly, without floating-point multiplication, accepting 0 to 2 decimals ("12", "12.5", "12.50") and throwing a RangeError for anything else.
questions.explain: Working on the digits keeps the arithmetic in whole numbers: Number("1150.15") * 100 is 115015.00000000001. padEnd turns "5" into "50" kobo.

questions.q: Write toCustomerResponse(customer) that returns only id, email, fullName and phone, building a new object field by field, so the password hash can never leak.
questions.explain: Returning customer itself would compile (structural typing) and leak the hash. A new literal contains only what you list, and adding a property that the response type lacks becomes a compile error.

questions.q: Without a library, write a type guard isOrderRow(value: unknown): value is OrderRow for rows with id (integer), status (one of four values) and note (string or null, but present). Then count the valid rows.
questions.explain: Row 2 has a status the type does not allow, row 3 is missing note entirely, and row 4 has a fractional id. filter(isOrderRow) also narrows the array's type to OrderRow[], so r.id is typed.

questions.q: Write toInterface(table, columns) that turns column metadata (as read from information_schema.columns) into the text of a row interface. Map int4 to number, int8 to string (the pg driver), text to string, timestamptz to Date, anything else to unknown, and add | null for nullable columns.
questions.explain: The mapping table is where the driver's behaviour is written down once. jsonb becomes unknown on purpose: its shape must be validated before use.

questions.q: Build a safe list query. Write buildOrderQuery(filter) for { customerId: number; status?: string; sort: "newest" | "biggest" }: values go into params as $1, $2…, and the sort comes from a fixed map. Return { sql, params }.
questions.explain: The injection attempt stays a harmless parameter value. Only text from ORDER_BY, which you wrote, ever becomes SQL, and the union type makes an unknown sort a compile error.

questions.q: Ids arrive from URLs as strings. Write parseOrderId(raw) that returns a branded OrderId for a positive whole number within the integer column's range (up to 2147483647), and null otherwise.
questions.explain: Parsing is the one place where a plain value may become an OrderId. Checking the range too avoids sending PostgreSQL a value that fails with "out of range for type integer" (a 500) instead of a clean 404.
